paper_title: Choosing Quantized Code LLMs by File Size and Energy per Solved Task

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A developer running a code assistant on a laptop downloads one model file, and local inference moves the energy of every request onto that machine. A common rule says a larger model at lower precision tends to beat a smaller one at higher precision. We ran 24 GGUF files of Qwen2.5-Coder at four sizes on a fanless MacBook Air M2 and priced each in energy per solved task on 542 EvalPlus tasks. The result is a selection guide indexed by Ollama's listed file size, with an evidence label on each pick. At 1 and 2 GB it picks the q4_K_M files of the 1.5B and 3B models, both on the correctness and energy frontier under every accounting. At 3 GB as listed, the larger-model rule picks 7B-q2_K, the only measured 7B file that fits, and there it does not pay. That file brings no significant gain in solves over the 2 GB pick, 3B-q4_K_M, and the 90% CI limits any 3B-q4_K_M deficit to 2.4 points. Yet 7B-q2_K needs 2.03 times the energy per solved task on CPU, GPU and memory rails, or 1.66 to 1.81 times on whole-system power. On HumanEval+, five alternating session pairs give a ratio of 1.925 against 1.956 in the main grid. At 8 GB, 7B-q6_K buys a significant gain over the 2 GB pick at a higher energy price. From 1.5B up, q4_K_M trails the highest precision measured at its size by less than 3 points (90% CI). We release per-task results, power logs and the analysis script.

sections.title: Start
sections.content: Aditi Patodiya Independent Researcher Email: aditi.patodia31@gmail.com AbstractA developer running code assistant on laptop downloads one model ﬁle, and local inference moves the energy of every request onto that machine. common rule says larger model at lower precision tends to beat smaller one at higher precision. We ran 24 GGUF ﬁles of Qwen2.5-Coder at four sizes on fanless MacBook Air M2 and priced each in energy per solved task on 542 EvalPlus tasks. The result is selection guide indexed by Ollamas listed ﬁle size, with an evidence label on each pick. At 1 and 2 GB it picks the q4_K_M ﬁles of the 1.5B and 3B models, both on the correctness and energy frontier under every accounting. At 3 GB as listed, the larger-model rule picks 7B-q2_K, the only measured 7B ﬁle that ﬁts, and there it does not pay. That ﬁle brings no signiﬁcant gain in solves over the 2 GB pick, 3B-q4_K_M, and the 90% CI limits any 3B-q4_K_M deﬁcit to 2.4 points. Yet 7B-q2_K needs 2.03 times the energy per solved task on CPU, GPU and memory rails, or 1.66 to 1.81 times on whole-system power. On HumanEval+, ﬁve alternating session pairs give ratio of 1.925 against 1.956 in the main grid. At 8 GB, 7B-q6_K buys signiﬁcant gain over the 2 GB pick at higher energy price. From 1.5B up, q4_K_M trails the highest precision measured at its size by less than 3 points (90% CI). We release per-task results, power logs and the analysis script. Index Termsgreen software, energy efﬁciency, large language models for code, quantization, GGUF k-quants, local inference, energy per solved task, model selection I. INTRODUCTION developer who runs code assistant on laptop downloads one model ﬁle. That ﬁle ﬁxes model size and quantization recipe. Ollama ships each size of model family under several recipe tags [1]. tag names recipe and not bit count: the 0.5B-q3_K_M ﬁle stores 5.66 effective bits per weight (BPW), and the 7B-q2_K ﬁle stores 3.16. The download is also an energy choice, because local inference moves the energy of code assistance onto the developers machine. Recent studies measure that energy for local code models and ﬁnd that the choice of model moves it [2], [3]. Cunha et al. [2] guide the choice of model and prompt. With the code family and prompt ﬁxed, developer still has to pick ﬁle that ﬁts size budget, and that is the choice we price. common rule guides the size choice. larger model at lower precision tends to beat smaller model at higher precision [3][5], and at ﬁxed total of bits four-bit precision is almost universally optimal [6]. Song et al. report performance threshold for this rule near 3.5 effective BPW on Submitted to GREENS 2027, the 11th International Workshop on Green and Sustainable Software at ICSE 2027. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible. general models [4]. We ask where the rule fails to pay on these code tasks once energy per solved task is counted. We price ﬁles in energy per solved task and treat it as the developers cost, since developer pays for working code. We measured 24 shipped GGUF ﬁles of Qwen2.5-CoderInstruct at four sizes on fanless MacBook Air M2. Every ﬁle ran the same 542 EvalPlus tasks. We compare solves task by task with exact paired tests. For the key step of the guide, 3B-q4_K_M against 7B-q2_K (the anchor pair), we also ran ﬁve alternating session pairs. Table II gives the resulting guide. At 1 GB listed-size budget it picks 1.5B-q4_K_M, and at 2 GB it picks 3Bq4_K_M. Both stay on the correctness and energy frontier under every accounting. At 3 GB as listed, the larger-model rule picks 7B-q2_K, the only measured 7B ﬁle that ﬁts, and there it does not pay. RQ1 (within size). What does each step down the quantization ladder cost in solved tasks and in energy per solved task at each of the four sizes? RQ2 (across sizes at budget). For listed ﬁle-size budget, which ﬁle solves the most tasks, and which ﬁles sit on the correctness and energy frontier with margin large enough to recommend them? RQ3 (the anchor step). Where does the larger-model rule to pay, and does the energy price of that step hold fail across alternating repeated sessions and change of energy accounting? The paper makes three contributions. C1. selection guide for local code LLMs. The guide is indexed by the ﬁle size Ollama lists, at budgets of 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 8 GB. For each budget it names the ﬁle that solves the most tasks among the 24 tested, its energy per solved task and its in-budget runner-up. Every budget pick and every rule that rests on comparison carries an evidence label that says whether it comes from the repeat, correctness test or pointestimate energy margin (Table II, Sec. V). C2. The anchor step at 2 to 3 GB, priced and repeated. 3B-q4_K_M solves 366 tasks against 363 for 7B-q2_K, ﬁle of 3.16 effective BPW, below the threshold Song et al. report. The 90% CI limits any 3B-q4_K_M deﬁcit to 2.4 points. The 7B ﬁle needs 2.03 times the energy per solved task (1.66 to 1.81 under whole-system accounting). On HumanEval+, ﬁve alternating session pairs give ratio of 1.925 against 1.956 for those tasks in the main grid. C3. regenerable price list for 24 shipped ﬁles. For every ﬁle we report effective bits per weight and energy per solved task beside energy per token. The released script regenerates every measured number. II. BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK A. What GGUF tag does and does not tell you The llama.cpp runtime runs quantized models stored as GGUF ﬁles [7]. Its k-quant recipes mix several tensor types within one ﬁle [8]. At 1.5B and above, tag such as q4_K_M names the recipe of most quantized tensors, while some stay at higher precision. At 0.5B the tag names minority: the q4_K_M ﬁle holds 12 q4_K tensors of 169, and the q6_K ﬁle holds 24 q6_K tensors, the rest q8_0. The effective BPW of ﬁle therefore departs from the number in its tag. The 0.5B-q3_K_M ﬁle holds no three-bit tensors and stores 5.66 BPW. B. Energy and correctness of local code LLMs Cunha et al. [2] benchmark ﬁve local LLMs on code tasks at GREENS 2026. Each model runs as one GGUF ﬁle at its own quantization level, on HumanEval-X and MBPP+, with CPU-only inference through llama.cpp on an Intel Core i78700 machine. They show that models trade accuracy against energy, and that the choice of model and of prompting both move energy and run time, so developer should make the two choices together. We hold one code family and one zeroshot prompt ﬁxed and vary model size and k-quant recipe on the GPU of fanless laptop. Energy per solved task is already in use. Abkin et al. [9] report energy per veriﬁed agent task with bootstrap intervals. TU Delft course study [10] reports energy per correct MBPP+ solution, and Saad-Falcon et al. [5] report accuracy per joule. Alizadeh et al. [3], [11] relate energy to code accuracy for Ollama fp16, q8 and q4 tags on laptop GPU and an A100, with Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B and 7B in the later study. They ﬁnd quantized large models ahead of full-precision medium ones, and the later study ﬁnds most Pareto-optimal points quantized. Our fp16 result agrees on fanless Apple laptop. Their ladder stops at q4 and reports energy per token or per workload, while ours continues to q3_K_M and q2_K and prices each ﬁle per solved task. On Ollama, quantized tags used less energy than fp16 [3], [11], while two studies on Hugging Face Transformers report that quantization raised energy [12], [13]. Our ﬁles sit on the Ollama side. Husom et al. [14] proﬁle quantized Ollama models at several quantization levels on Raspberry Pi. Rajput and Sharma ﬁnd GGML and GGUF the most energy-efﬁcient of ﬁve quantization methods [15]. Wei et al. [16] quantized code models to cut resource use and carbon footprint, and ran them on an M1 MacBook Pro. Afrin et al. [17] compare six quantization methods for Qwen2.5-Coder and CodeLlama. Shi et al. (Ditto) [18] score EvalPlus tasks and estimate energy per token from throughput at ﬁxed 18 on an Apple M4, where we read rail power per task. Giagnorio et al. [19] and Nyamsuren [20] ﬁnd four-bit precision good trade for code and steep loss at 2 bits. Giagnorio et al. also ﬁnd that large 2-bit models can beat smaller fullprecision ones, with no general trend, and Nyamsuren ﬁnds small fp16 models of similar size near the level of 2-bit 7B models on Lua. Neither measures energy. Thangarajah et al. serve Qwen2.5-Coder-3B through Ollama and ﬁnd that q4_K_M keeps its fp16 quality on code completion [21]. Our ladder agrees at 3B. At 7B it agrees with their advice for models of 3B or more. At 1.5B, where they advise q8_0, we ﬁnd q4_K_M equivalent to fp16 within 3 points. Melton [22] tests MLX four-bit ﬁles, including Qwen2.5Coder, on the same 542 EvalPlus tasks without measuring energy, and ﬁnds signiﬁcant loss at 1.5B and 3B but not at 7B. MLX also quantizes embeddings and the output head to four bits, while the q4_K_M ﬁles here store 5.08 and 4.99 effective bits per weight at those sizes, so two nominal fourbit ﬁles need not store the same bits. Song et al. [4] ﬁnd that heavily quantized larger models beat smaller high-precision ones on general models, with performance threshold near 3.5 effective bits per weight. Our 7B-q2_K ﬁle stores 3.16, below that threshold. Our question sits between these lines of work: one code family, priced in solved tasks and joules, ﬁle by ﬁle at size budget. C. Energy measurement on macOS Apples powermetrics tool reports component power that its manual describes as estimated [23]. The macmon tool reads the same IOReport counters without sudo [24]. Cruzs guide asks energy experiments to repeat and shufﬂe their runs [25]. In every repeat we ran, outputs repeated byte for byte (Sec. III-F), so those repeats bought energy precision alone. The paired repeat alternates the two ﬁles behind our selection guides key rule. III. STUDY DESIGN A. Files We study Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct at 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B and 7B parameters [26]. Every size runs q3_K_M, q4_K_M, q5_K_M, q6_K and q8_0. The 0.5B to 3B sizes also run fp16, and 7B alone adds q2_K, to trace the low end at the largest size. That gives 24 ﬁles. 7B was not run at fp16, which lists at about 15 GB on this 16 GB machine, so q8_0 is its highest precision measured. We use the registry tags as pulled and identify each ﬁle by its digest, because GGUF ﬁle need not record how it was built [27]. Effective BPW comes from the runtimes load log, the listed size from ollama list, and ﬁle bytes from the registry manifests for four ﬁles, the anchor pair among them, and from the load log plus metadata for the rest. We index budgets by the size Ollama lists, because developer sees it before download. Budgets are ﬁle sizes, not memory, and Rule 10 gives the headroom to leave for the runtime. B. Runtime and machine All ﬁles ran on Ollama 0.32.6 with its llama.cpp runner on Metal [1], [7]. The machine is fanless MacBook Air M2 with 16 GB of uniﬁed memory, under macOS 26.5, on AC power. Decoding takes the top-scoring token at temperature zero with ﬁxed seed, under Ollamas default repeat penalty of 1.1 over the last 64 tokens, and each task gets one sample. We call this greedy decoding. The context holds 2,048 tokens, and each answer has at most 768 new tokens. Files ran one at time in ﬁxed order, by size and then recipe, with one session per benchmark. We call these runs the main grid. C. Tasks and scoring The tasks are EvalPlus HumanEval+ (164 tasks) and MBPP+ (378 tasks), 542 tasks pooled [28][30]. task is solved when its sanitized solution passes both the base and the plus tests of EvalPlus. Correctness comes from serial re-evaluation of the stored solutions, covering every failed task and seeded 3% sample of passes, not new generation. to pass, It changed 9 outcomes in 8 ﬁles, all from fail with 0 on HumanEval+. No sampled pass ﬂipped, which supports leaving the other passes as scored. These correctness observations also supplied the tuning data of our registryscreening study [31]. This paper adds the energy and ﬁleselection analysis of those runs and the paired energy repeat. D. Energy In the main grid the macmon tool samples the CPU, GPU and memory rails once per second [24]. task window runs from the request to the response. We use count rule: each macmon sample inside task window counts once, at 1 s. Marginal power is rail power above an idle median of 0.509 W. Energy per solved task (J/solve) is the pooled marginal energy of both benchmark runs divided by the pooled solves. We report energy per output token (mJ/token) beside it. J/solve intervals are 95% task-bootstrap intervals within the maingrid sessions (B = 100,000, seed 20260810), printed in whole joules. For whole-system view we use macmons system power under three idle choices: pooled median, cleanidle median and no subtraction. In that view each sample is weighted by its gap to the previous one, with long gaps capped. We print that view as range, and we say under every accounting when point estimate holds across the rails and this view, under each idle choice and sample weighting we computed. Gap weighting moves J/solve by under 1% on every ﬁle and leaves the rails frontier unchanged. E. Statistics and the headline rule Paired tests of no difference use the exact McNemar test on the discordant tasks [32]. Holm correction [33] runs within each size for adjacent steps. Over the four sizes it runs in two separate families: the endpoints, and q4_K_M against the highest precision measured. Budget picks and the gains against the 2 GB pick are post hoc and chosen from the same data, so we correct them with Holm over all 276 pairs of the 24 ﬁles, which covers any pair chosen after seeing the results. Intervals on pass-rate differences come from task bootstrap computed exactly, with no Monte Carlo error, and are unadjusted. Equivalence (two one-sided tests [34]) and non-inferiority use margin of 3 points (about 16 of tasks), chosen after seeing the data. It lies below the smallest gain from 3B to 7B at matched recipe (5.2 points), and every verdict in Table III is unchanged for any margin from 2.6 to 3.1 points. Two ﬁles are equivalent when the 90% CI of their difference, which matches the two one-sided 5% tests, lies inside 3 points. q4_K_M is non-inferior when the upper 90% bound of the top-minus-q4_K_M difference is below 3 points. These readings rest on unadjusted intervals. Over the four sizes under Holm, paired score test [35] of non-inferiority gives adjusted 0.051, <0.001 and 0.051 at 1.5B, 3B and 7B. The bootstrap tail at +3 points gives 0.041, <0.001 and 0.041. Simultaneous evidence at 1.5B and 7B therefore depends on the method. For the anchor pair, 3B-q4_K_M is non-inferior when the lower 90% bound of 3B minus 7B lies above 3 points. Signiﬁcance rests on the Holm-adjusted values. The frontier is the non-dominated set over all 24 ﬁles on pooled pass rate (higher is better) and J/solve (lower is better). frontier ﬁles margin is how far its J/solve could rise before another ﬁle dominates it. An off-frontier ﬁles margin is how far its J/solve would have to fall to join. step to larger model pays when no smaller ﬁle dominates the ﬁle it buys. We headline an energy difference only if its margin is at least 40% or the paired repeat covers it. This is an exploratory screening heuristic that we set after the main grid. Speed can move between sessions with outputs ﬁxed: repeat of 1.5B-q4_K_M on HumanEval+, run without power logging, reproduced 164 of 164 outputs byte for byte, while median time 21.0%. As decode speed moved +23.6% and wall rough calibration, each ﬁles two power-logged sessions, which also differ in benchmark, differ in rail energy per token by at most 19.5% (median 3.7%). Compounded over both ﬁles of comparison, that swing is factor of 1.43, and every margin we headline clears it as ratio (smallest 1.44). The largest block swing in the paired repeat, 1.24 under macOS background work, stays below that factor. The labels do not change for any threshold from 33% to 40%. F. Repeats In every repeat we ran, the outputs were byte-identical under greedy decoding. That holds for 164 of 164 outputs in the 1.5B repeat, for all 10 blocks of the paired repeat against the main grid, and for all 50 outputs of 3B-q3_K_M repeat on HumanEval+. The guides picks are the ﬁles that solve the most tasks, so in these repeats session effects touched energy and speed, not the picks. The grids ﬁxed order ties size to time of day, so the paired repeat alternates the two anchor ﬁles. We chose this pair after the main grid: it joins the 2 GB pick to the smallest 7B ﬁle, the ﬁrst ﬁle of the larger model above that budget. The repeat ran ﬁve alternating pairs (AB BA AB BA AB) of 3B-q4_K_M (A) and 7B-q2_K (B) in one night. Each letter is one block, run of one ﬁle over all 164 tasks, preceded by cooldown gate of at least ﬁve minutes, until the CPU reached 45C or below. The repeat runs on HumanEval+, the benchmark with the lower main-grid ratio (1.95 against 2.11 on MBPP+ under the count rule), so it tests the smaller gap. Repeat energy, sampled about every 200 ms, uses the gap weighting of Sec. III-D, and so does the main-grid reference value for the repeat. block was valid if it ran all 164 tasks with outputs byte-identical to the main grid, stayed on AC power throughout, and had power samples over at least 98% of the duration of its task windows. valid block was ﬂagged if it was charging, the display was on, thermal pressure rose above zero or Low Power Mode was on. The validity rule, the ﬂag rule and the analysis were ﬁxed before the run, in the released scripts. The analysis is the geometric mean of the per-pair J/solve ratio (B over A), with 95% t-interval on log R. All 10 blocks were valid. IV. RESULTS A. RQ1: q4_K_M holds from 1.5B up From 1.5B up, q4_K_M trails the highest precision measured at its size by less than 3 points (90% CI; Table III, part A). Within that margin q4_K_M is equivalent to fp16 at 1.5B and to q8_0, the highest precision measured, at 7B. At 3B it is non-inferior to fp16: it trails by at most 0.6 points and may be up to 3.1 points better. At 0.5B, non-inferiority is not shown, and the loss is not signiﬁcant after Holm (p 0.142; raw 0.036). Part of Table III asks what the whole ladder costs, from the highest precision down to the lowest rung, and the answer differs by size. The difference is signiﬁcant after Holm at 0.5B (+5.0 points, fp16 against q3_K_M) and at 7B (+6.8 points, q8_0 against q2_K), and not at 1.5B (+2.2 points). At 7B, the step from q2_K to q3_K_M (raw 0.011) is not signiﬁcant after Holm (part D). The 3B-q3_K_M ﬁle solves 7 of 542 tasks, so the 3B difference, fp16 against q3_K_M, is +64.9 points. For this model the registry ﬁle is tensor-identical to plain uncalibrated llama.cpp rebuild, and importance-matrix quantization partly restores it [31]. The ﬁle stays in every statistic. Within each size, the cheapest ﬁle per solve leads the next one by 6.3% at 0.5B, 14.1% at 1.5B, 24.5% at 3B and 3.2% at 7B. All four gaps fall below 40%, so this stands as pattern: q4_K_M is among the cheapest working ﬁles per solve at 1.5B and 3B, and at 7B it costs 3.2% more per solve than q2_K. B. RQ2: The 1 GB and 2 GB picks hold the frontier Within each listed budget the ﬁle that solves the most tasks is 0.5B-q5_K_M, 1.5B-q4_K_M, 3B-q4_K_M, 7B-q3_K_M and 7B-q6_K (Table II). The 1 GB and 2 GB picks also stay on the point-estimate frontier under every accounting (Table I, Fig. 1). The rails frontier has 6 members: 0.5B-q3_K_M, 1.5Bq4_K_M, 3B-q4_K_M, 3B-q5_K_M, 7B-q4_K_M, 7B-q6_K. Under system power the low end changes: 0.5B-q3_K_M leaves and the frontier has 8 members. The other ﬁve railsfrontier members stay on it under every accounting. 7B-q6_K is on the frontier only because it has the top pass rate. At 1.5B and 3B, fp16 stays off the frontier under every accounting. On the rails it would need 43% and 40% less energy per solve to join. Table III, part E, gives the systempower margins, and at 1.5B the dominating ﬁle there is q6_K. 7B-q2_K sits off the frontier: 3B-q4_K_M dominates it, and Fig. 1. Pooled pass rate against energy per solved task (log scale) for all 24 ﬁles, each from its main-grid sessions. The step line is the rails frontier, and ﬁlled markers stay on it under every accounting. Rings mark the ﬁve budget picks with their listed size. labeled link joins the anchor pair, 3B-q4_K_M and 7B-q2_K. The 3B-q3_K_M ﬁle sits off scale (4,708 J, 1.3%). the 7B ﬁles energy per solve would have to fall 50.9% to join. Three other comparisons are too close to rank without repeats (Rule 9). At matched recipes from q4_K_M to q8_0, the 7B ﬁle costs 2.10 to 2.13 times the energy per solve of its 3B sibling for 5.2 to 8.3 more points, and at q3_K_M the ratio is 0.04, because the 3B-q3_K_M ﬁle solves so few tasks. 3B-q4_K_M reaches 90.8% of the best score measured, that of 7B-q6_K, at 38% of that ﬁles energy per solve. Computed in ﬁle bytes (decimal GB), the picks at all ﬁve budgets are unchanged, and Rule 10 gives the three that move once the runtimes logged buffers count. The ﬁve stable members stay on the frontier when energy per task or per output token replaces energy per solve, and only the 0.5B end changes. Over working ﬁles the ranks of energy per solve stay close to those of energy per token, and the difference falls where the budgets are. Per token, 1.5B-q4_K_M costs 1.98 times 0.5B-q3_K_M, while per solve the two sit within 1.2%, and four 0.5B ﬁles that per-token frontier would keep fall off the per-solve frontier. C. RQ3: At 3 GB the larger model does not pay At 3 GB as listed, the larger-model rule picks 7B-q2_K, the only measured 7B ﬁle that ﬁts, and there it does not pay (Table III, part C). The rule pays below this step: 3B-q4_K_M solves 366 tasks against 316 for 1.5B-q4_K_M (post hoc, allpairs Holm <0.001). Against 7B-q2_K, 3B-q4_K_M solves 134 to 131 on HumanEval+, and both solve 232 on MBPP+. As in Vallecillos-Ruiz et al. [13], we report solved-set overlap: 48 tasks are solved only by 3B-q4_K_M and 45 only by 7Bq2_K (exact McNemar 0.836). On HumanEval+, the energy price of the step holds across alternating sessions  (Fig. 2)  . 7B-q2_K cost more per solved task in all ﬁve pairs. The ﬁve pairs give ratio of 1.925 (95% CI 1.718 to 2.157), against 1.956 for the main-grid HumanEval+ sessions with the same gap weighting. The ﬁvepair mean lies 1.5% below that value, and post hoc value without pair 1 (Sec. VI) lies 2.6% above it. Without pair 1, the AB and BA pairs give similar means, 2.005 and 2.006. Under system power the paired-repeat ratio is 1.86 (95% CI 1.66 to 2.09). In the paired-repeat sessions 3B-q4_K_M decoded 2.03 times as fast as 7B-q2_K (95% CI 2.00 to 2.06), and 7Bq2_K took 1.98 times the wall time (1.92 to 2.03). Energy, decode speed and wall time moved by about the same factor, so in these sessions the larger ﬁle costs more because it runs longer at similar rail power. The cheaper ﬁle was also the faster one, so picking it gave up no response time. V. THE SELECTION GUIDE Four prices decide the download. From the 1 GB pick to the 2 GB pick, 1.76 times the energy per solve buys 9.2 more points. From the 2 GB pick to 7B-q2_K, 2.03 times (1.66 to 1.81 under whole-system accounting) buys no signiﬁcant gain. From the 2 GB pick, 7B-q4_K_M costs 2.10 times for 5.5 more points and 7B-q6_K costs 2.64 times for 6.8 more. Table II gives the picks. developer who budgets joules as well as gigabytes has reason to stop at 3B-q4_K_M. The next ﬁle up in solves, 3B-q5_K_M, costs 45.8% more per solve for one more task. Along the stable frontier, in single sessions, each extra solved task costs about 259 from 1.5B-q4_K_M to 3B-q4_K_M and about 1,077 from 3B-q4_K_M to 7B-q4_K_M, about four times as much, and more under whole-system accounting. 1) Read the listed size and the measured result, not the tag. The 0.5B-q3_K_M ﬁle stores 5.66 effective bits per weight and the 7B-q2_K ﬁle 3.16, and Rule 10 shows tag whose ﬁle fails most tasks, so the digits in tag give neither the bits ﬁle stores nor its correctness. 2) At 1 GB budget, take 1.5B-q4_K_M [lead unresolved; frontier member]. It stays on the frontier under every accounting, and Table II gives its frontier margin and in-budget runner-up. 3) At 2 GB budget, take 3B-q4_K_M [signiﬁcant lead; frontier member]. It leads the best 1.5B ﬁle by 9.2 points and stays on the frontier under every accounting, so the step from 1 GB to 2 GB trades energy for points. 4) Do not spend the next gigabyte on 7B-q2_K [repeated]. It solves 363 tasks against 366 for 3B-q4_K_M, and the 90% CI limits any 3B-q4_K_M deﬁcit to 2.4 points. It needs 2.03 times the energy per solve (1.66 to 1.81 under whole-system accounting). On HumanEval+, ﬁve alternating session pairs give ratio of 1.925 against 1.956 in the main grid (Sec. IV-C). 5) Skip fp16 at 1.5B and 3B [margin 40%]. It stays off the frontier under every accounting (Table III, part E). 6) From 1.5B up, start at q4_K_M [non-inferior at the post hoc margin]. Against the highest precision measured it costs 39.3 against 69.1 per solve at 1.5B, 69.4 against 116.1 at 3B and 145.7 against 187.1 at 7B, where the gap falls below 40%. 7) At 4 GB budget, choose by what you are budgeting [leads unresolved]. For solved tasks, 7B-q3_K_M leads: 71.6% against 67.5% for the 2 GB pick. For joules, stay on the 2 GB pick: 69 against 187 per solve. 8) At an 8 GB budget, move up only if the extra points are worth the energy [lead unresolved]. The 7B ﬁles from q4_K_M to q6_K are not separated on solves, and 7B-q6_K leads them by at most 2.95 points (90% CI). Against the 2 GB pick, the gain of 7B-q6_K stays signiﬁcant under Holm over all ﬁle pairs (p 0.010), and those of 7B-q4_K_M and 7B-q3_K_M do not (p 0.103 and 1.000). 9) Where lead is unresolved or an energy ranking unreplicated, let the other axis decide. At 7B, q4_K_M costs 3.2% more per solve than q2_K [energy ranking unreplicated] and solves 396 tasks against 363. Its lead over q2_K stays signiﬁcant under Holm over all ﬁle pairs (p 0.031), so take q4_K_M when 4.70 GB ﬁts. This also covers the 0.5B recipes at 0.5 GB budget and two frontier calls too close to read: 0.5B-q3_K_M on by 1.2% and 7B-q8_0 off by 2.2%. 10) Smoke-test downloads and leave headroom. The 3Bq3_K_M tag, non-functional in [31], ﬁts the 2 GB budget at 1.60 GB but solves 7 of 542 tasks. Per token it ranks 14th of 24, and per solved task it ranks 24th, at 68 times the energy per solve of its q4_K_M sibling. Unusable q2_K ﬁles of 3B Qwen2.5 models have been reported before [21], [36]. Leave headroom above the listed size, because the runtimes buffers add 2.7 to 19.2% at load. If free memory is the limit and not ﬁle size, those buffers, lower bound on the runtimes allocation, move the 1, 2 and 4 GB picks in decimal GB to smaller ﬁles: 1.5Bq3_K_M, 1.5B-q4_K_M and 3B-q5_K_M. Counted in GiB, that bound moves only the 1 GB pick. As of November 2026, the 1 GB and 2 GB picks are the ﬁles behind the registrys default tags qwen2.5-coder:1.5b and qwen2.5-coder:3b, and 7B-q4_K_M is the ﬁle behind qwen2.5-coder:7b. From 1.5B up, then, developer who takes sizes default tag stays on the frontier, and 7Bq2_K, fp16 and the 3B-q3_K_M tag are all off-default.

sections.title: Our result
sections.content: is consistent with the four-bit optimum of Dettmers and Zettlemoyer [6], for one code family with executed tests and energy. The q4_K_M ﬁles we favor store 5.08, 4.99 and 4.91 effective bits from 1.5B to 7B, so the shipped q4_K_M ﬁle is closer to ﬁve. Registries could print effective bits per weight beside each tag. leaderboard column of energy per token should carry solve count beside it, since ﬁle can sit mid-table per token and still fail the tests. team can measure its own grid with the released harness and adapt the analysis script to rebuild the guide. For team that standardizes on this family on similar machines, the guide narrows trial downloads to lookup by size budget that carries correctness and energy together. For research, these results change what study of quantized code models should print. It should report effective bits beside tags, because threshold stated in bits cannot be tested by tag. It should price per solved task beside per token, because four working 0.5B ﬁles that per-token frontier keeps fall off the per-solve frontier, and Rule 10 shows how far the two can part. Under greedy decoding it should spend repeats on energy at decision steps, because in every repeat we ran outputs repeated byte for byte (Sec. III-F) while energy and speed moved. VI. THREATS TO VALIDITY Energy measurement. Energy comes from Apples IOReport estimates read by macmon [23], [24], with no external power meter. Because the CPU, GPU and memory rails cover 28 to 53% of macmons system power, we compare ﬁles on one machine as ratios and do not set absolute joules beside RAPL or NVML studies. System power includes the display, which stayed on in the main grid and off in the repeat, so we do not compare system power between them. Sessions. Each grid ﬁle ran in one session per benchmark, back to back with no rest between sessions and in ﬁxed order by size and then recipe, so size and recipe align with time of day and with how long the machine had been under load. Other applications were open during the main grid. The paired repeat alternates the anchor ﬁles, which reduces the alignment between ﬁle and run order: with cooldown gate before every block, its ﬁve-pair HumanEval+ ratio lies 1.5% below the main-grid value. Paired repeat. The paired repeat covers the anchor pair on HumanEval+ in one night on AC power. Thermal pressure stayed at Heavy for 90 to 97% of every block in both arms, so all 5 pairs were ﬂagged under the pre-speciﬁed rule and no unﬂagged subset exists. We record this as telemetry and draw no thermal conclusion. Browser and assistant apps were open, and automatic updates were on with none installed. Pair 1 overlapped macOS media analysis, and Spotlight indexing ran just before it. Without pair 1, post hoc check gives 2.005 (1.971 to 2.041). The pre-speciﬁed ﬁve-pair ﬁgure keeps pair 1, stays primary and is the lower of the two. Statistics. The 3-point equivalence and non-inferiority margin was chosen after seeing the data, and the 40% rule of Sec. III-E was set after the main grid. J/solve intervals capture task sampling within the main-grid sessions. Between-session variation comes from the paired repeat for the anchor pair on HumanEval+ in one night, and, as rougher guide, from the two benchmark sessions of each ﬁle, which also differ in tasks. Cross-size energy outside the anchor pair comes from single sessions. The frontier uses point estimates, and under system power 1.5B-q4_K_M keeps its place by one solved task over 1.5B-q6_K, which lists outside the 1 GB budget. Idle baselines. The clean-idle baseline moves J/solve by 1.7 to 4.0% and leaves the anchor ratio at 2.03. In the repeat, using the end-of-night idle or the main-grid idle instead of the start-of-night idle gives 1.929 and 1.926. Population. The study covers one code family, one runtime, one fanless machine, Python tasks, one zero-shot prompt and greedy decoding. The grid covers 24 of the 60 instruct recipes the registry lists from 0.5B to 7B. It leaves out other recipes at these sizes, such as q4_K_S and q4_0, and larger sizes, including the 14B ﬁles that list under 8 GB, so each pick is the best of the measured ﬁles. Picks may move for other families, runtimes, cooling designs or languages. Registry ﬁles. Files are registry tags as pulled and identiﬁed by digest (3B-q3_K_M blob 9bb5d28b, manifest 65ff2bc1), so re-pushed tag can be detected. Absolute scores. Our 7B-q8_0 ﬁle scores 84.1% on HumanEval+ and 69.3% on MBPP+, in line with Table 16 of the Qwen2.5-Coder report [26]. VII. CONCLUSION larger quantized code model is not automatically the better download, and tag does not tell developer which ﬁle that is. The picks are 1.5B-q4_K_M at 1 GB and 3B-q4_K_M at 2 GB, both on the frontier under every accounting. At the step from 2 to 3 GB the larger model does not pay: 7B-q2_K brings no signiﬁcant gain in solves over 3B-q4_K_M, and the 90% CI limits any 3B-q4_K_M deﬁcit to 2.4 points. The 7B ﬁle needs 2.03 times the energy per solve (1.66 to 1.81 on whole-system power). At 8 GB, 7B-q6_K buys signiﬁcant gain over the 2 GB pick at higher energy price. Registries could print effective bits beside each tag, and studies could price ﬁles per solved task beside per token. The ﬁle developer downloads is an energy decision as well as correctness one, made once and with no change to code or hardware.

sections.title: DATA AVAILABILITY
sections.content: The per-task correctness vectors, per-task energies, power logs, paired-repeat logs, ﬁle digests and the grid harness are in the artifact at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24016482. The script analysis/p1_numbers.py writes every measured number in this paper from hash-checked inputs and the four registry manifests it reads. fresh-directory run of the package on the study machine reproduced those numbers.
